evidence.title: OBR energy-import shock, real incomes and fiscal exposure
evidence.facts: The official October outlook describes a negative energy terms-of-trade shock. Central growth is around 1.25% in 2026 and 1% in 2027; 2027 is about half a percentage point below March. It projects CPI around 3.5% in 2027 and lower real disposable income than previously forecast. Fiscal consolidation is delayed, but the 2029-30 current-budget rule retains a GBP15 billion margin. Morgan analysis says the budget met fiscal-restraint expectations, gilts slightly outperformed peers and sterling received modest support. It reports substantial expected BoE tightening but no new BoE commitment. The delivered reassurance challenges using structural growth/fiscal headwinds alone as the current-session direction.

evidence.title: Australia trade prices: import-cost relief alongside higher export prices
evidence.facts: ABS September-quarter export prices rose 1.4% q/q and 6.3% y/y; import prices fell 1.1% q/q and rose 5.5% y/y. Export gains included gas +28.6%, coal +4.8% and cereals +5.7%, opposed by ores -6.4% and non-monetary gold -4.8%. Import declines included petroleum -8.7% and fertilisers -20.2%, opposed by office/ADP machines +7.3% and telecom equipment +4.1%. ABS attributes petroleum relief to improving supply during the quarter; this is not proof that current geopolitical threats are resolved. Lower import costs are a fresh offset to the inflation-path argument while export-price resilience supports external incomes. The export/import price ratio improved on these indexes; no national-accounts terms-of-trade actual or private inflow is asserted. Broker AU trade-price series were absent from the focused local snapshot; web calendar forecasts differ and are not treated as a unique consensus.

evidence.title: UK household borrowing slows; stronger business lending offsets the downside
evidence.facts: September net house-purchase mortgage approvals fell to 53,400 from revised August 54,800; remortgage approvals rose to 42,600 from 34,000. Net mortgage borrowing slowed to GBP3.9bn from revised GBP4.2bn, below the prior six-month GBP4.9bn average. Net consumer credit fell to GBP1.9bn from revised GBP2.7bn, slightly below the prior six-month GBP2.1bn average. Mortgage borrowing and consumer credit were below broker forecasts GBP5.363bn and GBP2.368bn; approvals exceeded the broker forecast 50.828k but were slightly below the separately attributed web survey 54.00k. Do not call approvals an unqualified surprise miss. New mortgage effective rates rose to 4.63% from 4.60%. Offsetting household softness, non-financial business bank borrowing rose to GBP9.3bn from GBP4.7bn, M4Lex net flow rose to GBP17.0bn from GBP9.9bn and PNFC bank loans to GBP10.6bn from GBP6.4bn. PNFC total net finance nevertheless slowed to GBP3.1bn from GBP8.5bn after redemptions/buybacks. M4ex money net flow slowed to GBP3.9bn from GBP16.9bn. Levels, net flows and annual growth are distinct; this is one release package, not independent votes. September observations predate the October 28 budget and do not measure its effect.

evidence.title: US Q3 domestic demand remains strong; monthly core persistence offsets quarterly disinflation
evidence.facts: Q3 advance real GDP grew 3.4% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, versus Q2 2.2% and the attributed web survey 3.2%; the broker-model forecast was 1.4% and is not consensus. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. evidence.title: US Q3 domestic demand remains strong; monthly core persistence offsets quarterly disinflation
evidence.facts: Q3 advance real GDP grew 3.4% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, versus Q2 2.2% and the attributed web survey 3.2%; the broker-model forecast was 1.4% and is not consensus. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. One combined package, not a count of components.

August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. evidence.title: UK household borrowing slows; stronger business lending offsets the downside
evidence.facts: September net house-purchase mortgage approvals fell to 53,400 from revised August 54,800; remortgage approvals rose to 42,600 from 34,000. Net mortgage borrowing slowed to GBP3.9bn from revised GBP4.2bn, below the prior six-month GBP4.9bn average. Net consumer credit fell to GBP1.9bn from revised GBP2.7bn, slightly below the prior six-month GBP2.1bn average. Mortgage borrowing and consumer credit were below broker forecasts GBP5.363bn and GBP2.368bn; approvals exceeded the broker forecast 50.828k but were slightly below the separately attributed web survey 54.00k. Do not call approvals an unqualified surprise miss. New mortgage effective rates rose to 4.63% from 4.60%. Offsetting household softness, non-financial business bank borrowing rose to GBP9.3bn from GBP4.7bn, M4Lex net flow rose to GBP17.0bn from GBP9.9bn and PNFC bank loans to GBP10.6bn from GBP6.4bn. PNFC total net finance nevertheless slowed to GBP3.1bn from GBP8.5bn after redemptions/buybacks. M4ex money net flow slowed to GBP3.9bn from GBP16.9bn. Levels, net flows and annual growth are distinct; this is one release package, not independent votes. September observations predate the October 28 budget and do not measure its effect.

evidence.title: BoC expected hike and cautious further-tightening path
evidence.facts: The BoC raised 25 bp to 2.50% on October 28, as broadly anticipated. It revised the growth outlook upward, with 2027/2028 GDP around 2%, and projected more persistent inflation: annual-average 2027 inflation about 3%, one percentage point above July, returning to target around mid-2028. Core remains near 2%, CPI excluding gasoline 2.2%, unemployment around 6.5%, excess supply persists and tariffs weigh on Q4. Further increases are conditional and officials will proceed carefully. RBC's October 28 analysis retains a 100 bp total cycle (three further hikes after October) conditional on resilience, while acknowledging no current-data urgency, already-priced term yields and growth downside relative to BoC projections. Financial Post reports Bloomberg-attributed December hike odds falling to 55% after the decision from 100% Tuesday; Canadian Press separately attributes 43% to LSEG Wednesday afternoon. These provider/time snapshots are not interchangeable or a directly refreshed curve. CIBC/Desjardins favour another hike in January and 2.75% peak, illustrating forecast disagreement. Stronger growth/income and a possible longer cycle are support; the reported negative near-term path repricing is material opposition to a current strengthening claim.

evidence.title: US Q3 domestic demand remains strong; monthly core persistence offsets quarterly disinflation
evidence.facts: Q3 advance real GDP grew 3.4% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, versus Q2 2.2% and the attributed web survey 3.2%; the broker-model forecast was 1.4% and is not consensus. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. One combined package, not a count of components.

evidence.title: BoC expected hike and cautious further-tightening path
evidence.facts: The BoC raised 25 bp to 2.50% on October 28, as broadly anticipated. It revised the growth outlook upward, with 2027/2028 GDP around 2%, and projected more persistent inflation: annual-average 2027 inflation about 3%, one percentage point above July, returning to target around mid-2028. Core remains near 2%, CPI excluding gasoline 2.2%, unemployment around 6.5%, excess supply persists and tariffs weigh on Q4. Further increases are conditional and officials will proceed carefully. RBC's October 28 analysis retains a 100 bp total cycle (three further hikes after October) conditional on resilience, while acknowledging no current-data urgency, already-priced term yields and growth downside relative to BoC projections. Financial Post reports Bloomberg-attributed December hike odds falling to 55% after the decision from 100% Tuesday; Canadian Press separately attributes 43% to LSEG Wednesday afternoon. These provider/time snapshots are not interchangeable or a directly refreshed curve. CIBC/Desjardins favour another hike in January and 2.75% peak, illustrating forecast disagreement. Stronger growth/income and a possible longer cycle are support; the reported negative near-term path repricing is material opposition to a current strengthening claim.

evidence.title: US Q3 domestic demand remains strong; monthly core persistence offsets quarterly disinflation
evidence.facts: Q3 advance real GDP grew 3.4% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, versus Q2 2.2% and the attributed web survey 3.2%; the broker-model forecast was 1.4% and is not consensus. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. One combined package, not a count of components.

Levels, net flows and annual growth are distinct; this is one release package, not independent votes. September observations predate the October 28 budget and do not measure its effect.

evidence.title: BoC expected hike and cautious further-tightening path
evidence.facts: The BoC raised 25 bp to 2.50% on October 28, as broadly anticipated. It revised the growth outlook upward, with 2027/2028 GDP around 2%, and projected more persistent inflation: annual-average 2027 inflation about 3%, one percentage point above July, returning to target around mid-2028. Core remains near 2%, CPI excluding gasoline 2.2%, unemployment around 6.5%, excess supply persists and tariffs weigh on Q4. Further increases are conditional and officials will proceed carefully. RBC's October 28 analysis retains a 100 bp total cycle (three further hikes after October) conditional on resilience, while acknowledging no current-data urgency, already-priced term yields and growth downside relative to BoC projections. Financial Post reports Bloomberg-attributed December hike odds falling to 55% after the decision from 100% Tuesday; Canadian Press separately attributes 43% to LSEG Wednesday afternoon. These provider/time snapshots are not interchangeable or a directly refreshed curve. CIBC/Desjardins favour another hike in January and 2.75% peak, illustrating forecast disagreement. Stronger growth/income and a possible longer cycle are support; the reported negative near-term path repricing is material opposition to a current strengthening claim.

evidence.title: RBNZ hold surprise and subsequent hawkish offset

The majority cited lower-than-expected inflation, smaller indirect fuel-price effects, subdued wages, weak consumption/investment and time to observe two previous hikes. Core near the upper target band and broader price increases were largely expected, rather than evidence of a fresh upside surprise. All members still see tighter policy likely, conditional on the outlook; the record explicitly allows future holds or easing if global demand deteriorates sharply. RNZ reports Westpac economist Eckhold observed the one-year swap rate down about 20 bp after the decision on October 28. That report is an attributed event-time observation, not a new/current October 29 yield measurement. Later conference remarks about further hikes and imported inflation are substantial opposition to weakness. Wholesale-to-retail rate pass-through and cost-to-CPI pass-through are distinct; no mechanical rate conclusion is drawn from either.

evidence.title: US Q3 domestic demand remains strong; monthly core persistence offsets quarterly disinflation
evidence.facts: Q3 advance real GDP grew 3.4% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, versus Q2 2.2% and the attributed web survey 3.2%; the broker-model forecast was 1.4% and is not consensus. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. One combined package, not a count of components.

evidence.title: UK household borrowing slows; stronger business lending offsets the downside
evidence.facts: September net house-purchase mortgage approvals fell to 53,400 from revised August 54,800; remortgage approvals rose to 42,600 from 34,000. Net consumer credit fell to GBP1.9bn from revised GBP2.7bn, slightly below the prior six-month GBP2.1bn average. Mortgage borrowing and consumer credit were below broker forecasts GBP5.363bn and GBP2.368bn; approvals exceeded the broker forecast 50.828k but were slightly below the separately attributed web survey 54.00k. Do not call approvals an unqualified surprise miss. New mortgage effective rates rose to 4.63% from 4.60%. Offsetting household softness, non-financial business bank borrowing rose to GBP9.3bn from GBP4.7bn, M4Lex net flow rose to GBP17.0bn from GBP9.9bn and PNFC bank loans to GBP10.6bn from GBP6.4bn. PNFC total net finance nevertheless slowed to GBP3.1bn from GBP8.5bn after redemptions/buybacks. M4ex money net flow slowed to GBP3.9bn from GBP16.9bn. Levels, net flows and annual growth are distinct; this is one release package, not independent votes. September observations predate the October 28 budget and do not measure its effect.

evidence.title: BoC expected hike and cautious further-tightening path

Core remains near 2%, CPI excluding gasoline 2.2%, unemployment around 6.5%, excess supply persists and tariffs weigh on Q4. Further increases are conditional and officials will proceed carefully. RBC's October 28 analysis retains a 100 bp total cycle (three further hikes after October) conditional on resilience, while acknowledging no current-data urgency, already-priced term yields and growth downside relative to BoC projections. Financial Post reports Bloomberg-attributed December hike odds falling to 55% after the decision from 100% Tuesday; Canadian Press separately attributes 43% to LSEG Wednesday afternoon. These provider/time snapshots are not interchangeable or a directly refreshed curve. CIBC/Desjardins favour another hike in January and 2.75% peak, illustrating forecast disagreement. Stronger growth/income and a possible longer cycle are support; the reported negative near-term path repricing is material opposition to a current strengthening claim.

evidence.title: US Q3 domestic demand remains strong; monthly core persistence offsets quarterly disinflation
evidence.facts: Q3 advance real GDP grew 3.4% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, versus Q2 2.2% and the attributed web survey 3.2%; the broker-model forecast was 1.4% and is not consensus. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. One combined package, not a count of components.

evidence.title: UK household borrowing slows; stronger business lending offsets the downside
evidence.facts: September net house-purchase mortgage approvals fell to 53,400 from revised August 54,800; remortgage approvals rose to 42,600 from 34,000. Net consumer credit fell to GBP1.9bn from revised GBP2.7bn, slightly below the prior six-month GBP2.1bn average. Mortgage borrowing and consumer credit were below broker forecasts GBP5.363bn and GBP2.368bn; approvals exceeded the broker forecast 50.828k but were slightly below the separately attributed web survey 54.00k. Do not call approvals an unqualified surprise miss. New mortgage effective rates rose to 4.63% from 4.60%. Offsetting household softness, non-financial business bank borrowing rose to GBP9.3bn from GBP4.7bn, M4Lex net flow rose to GBP17.0bn from GBP9.9bn and PNFC bank loans to GBP10.6bn from GBP6.4bn. PNFC total net finance nevertheless slowed to GBP3.1bn from GBP8.5bn after redemptions/buybacks. M4ex money net flow slowed to GBP3.9bn from GBP16.9bn. Levels, net flows and annual growth are distinct; this is one release package, not independent votes. September observations predate the October 28 budget and do not measure its effect.

evidence.title: BoC expected hike and cautious further-tightening path
evidence.facts: The BoC raised 25 bp to 2.50% on October 28, as broadly anticipated. It revised the growth outlook upward, with 2027/2028 GDP around 2%, and projected more persistent inflation: annual-average 2027 inflation about 3%, one percentage point above July, returning to target around mid-2028. Core remains near 2%, CPI excluding gasoline 2.2%, unemployment around 6.5%, excess supply persists and tariffs weigh on Q4. Further increases are conditional and officials will proceed carefully. RBC's October 28 analysis retains a 100 bp total cycle (three further hikes after October) conditional on resilience, while acknowledging no current-data urgency, already-priced term yields and growth downside relative to BoC projections. Financial Post reports Bloomberg-attributed December hike odds falling to 55% after the decision from 100% Tuesday; Canadian Press separately attributes 43% to LSEG Wednesday afternoon. These provider/time snapshots are not interchangeable or a directly refreshed curve. CIBC/Desjardins favour another hike in January and 2.75% peak, illustrating forecast disagreement. Stronger growth/income and a possible longer cycle are support; the reported negative near-term path repricing is material opposition to a current strengthening claim.

evidence.title: RBNZ hold surprise and subsequent hawkish offset
evidence.facts: The complete official October 28 record confirms a 4-3 hold at 2.75%, against widely expected October tightening. The majority cited lower-than-expected inflation, smaller indirect fuel-price effects, subdued wages, weak consumption/investment and time to observe two previous hikes. Core near the upper target band and broader price increases were largely expected, rather than evidence of a fresh upside surprise. All members still see tighter policy likely, conditional on the outlook; the record explicitly allows future holds or easing if global demand deteriorates sharply. RNZ reports Westpac economist Eckhold observed the one-year swap rate down about 20 bp after the decision on October 28. That report is an attributed event-time observation, not a new/current October 29 yield measurement. Later conference remarks about further hikes and imported inflation are substantial opposition to weakness. The October 29 Herald interview is now verified separately; this does not verify every scheduled broadcast. Wholesale-to-retail rate pass-through and cost-to-CPI pass-through are distinct; no mechanical rate conclusion is drawn from either.

Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. One combined package, not a count of components.
evidence.timing_note: Official releases state 8:30 AM EDT / 12:30 UTC (7:30 PM Jakarta). This is the publisher-declared release clock, not a measured first-publication second. PCE first verified here 12:30:24 UTC; complete GDP PDF first verified 12:32:11 UTC after stale/404 HTML routes.

evidence.title: BoC expected hike and cautious further-tightening path
evidence.facts: The BoC raised 25 bp to 2.50% on October 28, as broadly anticipated. It revised the growth outlook upward, with 2027/2028 GDP around 2%, and projected more persistent inflation: annual-average 2027 inflation about 3%, one percentage point above July, returning to target around mid-2028. Core remains near 2%, CPI excluding gasoline 2.2%, unemployment around 6.5%, excess supply persists and tariffs weigh on Q4. Further increases are conditional and officials will proceed carefully. RBC's October 28 analysis retains a 100 bp total cycle (three further hikes after October) conditional on resilience, while acknowledging no current-data urgency, already-priced term yields and growth downside relative to BoC projections. Financial Post reports Bloomberg-attributed December hike odds falling to 55% after the decision from 100% Tuesday; Canadian Press separately attributes 43% to LSEG Wednesday afternoon. These provider/time snapshots are not interchangeable or a directly refreshed curve. CIBC/Desjardins favour another hike in January and 2.75% peak, illustrating forecast disagreement. Stronger growth/income and a possible longer cycle are support; the reported negative near-term path repricing is material opposition to a current strengthening claim.

evidence.title: Australia trade prices: import-cost relief alongside higher export prices
evidence.facts: ABS September-quarter export prices rose 1.4% q/q and 6.3% y/y; import prices fell 1.1% q/q and rose 5.5% y/y. Export gains included gas +28.6%, coal +4.8% and cereals +5.7%, opposed by ores -6.4% and non-monetary gold -4.8%. Import declines included petroleum -8.7% and fertilisers -20.2%, opposed by office/ADP machines +7.3% and telecom equipment +4.1%. ABS attributes petroleum relief to improving supply during the quarter; this is not proof that current geopolitical threats are resolved. Lower import costs are a fresh offset to the inflation-path argument while export-price resilience supports external incomes. The export/import price ratio improved on these indexes; no national-accounts terms-of-trade actual or private inflow is asserted. Broker AU trade-price series were absent from the focused local snapshot; web calendar forecasts differ and are not treated as a unique consensus.

evidence.title: US Q3 domestic demand remains strong; monthly core persistence offsets quarterly disinflation
evidence.facts: Q3 advance real GDP grew 3.4% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, versus Q2 2.2% and the attributed web survey 3.2%; the broker-model forecast was 1.4% and is not consensus. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. One combined package, not a count of components.

evidence.title: UK household borrowing slows; stronger business lending offsets the downside
evidence.facts: September net house-purchase mortgage approvals fell to 53,400 from revised August 54,800; remortgage approvals rose to 42,600 from 34,000. Net mortgage borrowing slowed to GBP3.9bn from revised GBP4.2bn, below the prior six-month GBP4.9bn average. Net consumer credit fell to GBP1.9bn from revised GBP2.7bn, slightly below the prior six-month GBP2.1bn average. Mortgage borrowing and consumer credit were below broker forecasts GBP5.363bn and GBP2.368bn; approvals exceeded the broker forecast 50.828k but were slightly below the separately attributed web survey 54.00k. Do not call approvals an unqualified surprise miss. New mortgage effective rates rose to 4.63% from 4.60%. Offsetting household softness, non-financial business bank borrowing rose to GBP9.3bn from GBP4.7bn, M4Lex net flow rose to GBP17.0bn from GBP9.9bn and PNFC bank loans to GBP10.6bn from GBP6.4bn. PNFC total net finance nevertheless slowed to GBP3.1bn from GBP8.5bn after redemptions/buybacks. M4ex money net flow slowed to GBP3.9bn from GBP16.9bn. Levels, net flows and annual growth are distinct; this is one release package, not independent votes. September observations predate the October 28 budget and do not measure its effect.

These provider/time snapshots are not interchangeable or a directly refreshed curve. CIBC/Desjardins favour another hike in January and 2.75% peak, illustrating forecast disagreement. Stronger growth/income and a possible longer cycle are support; the reported negative near-term path repricing is material opposition to a current strengthening claim.

evidence.title: Australia CPI and RBA capacity reassessment
evidence.facts: ABS September headline CPI is 4.3% y/y versus 4.0% in August; monthly-series trimmed mean is 3.6% versus revised 3.5%. The RBA says labour conditions look tighter than previously judged despite higher unemployment, productivity is weak and domestic/international upside inflation risks have materialised. NAB shifted to a November 25 bp hike forecast. It reports quarterly trimmed mean 1.0% q/q and 3.7% y/y against attributed consensus 1.0%/3.6%. Monthly core was broadly expected; monthly and quarterly core series differ and are not competing actuals. No RBA November promise was made. In the same October 28 note, NAB expects a November hike to 4.85%, then a likely pause, describing policy as restrictive. It says the marginal September core reading was broadly expected and did not further fuel concern about more persistent components. This limits the inference from a likely near-term hike to a continuing sequence; it is an institutional forecast rather than RBA forward guidance.

evidence.title: Australia trade prices: import-cost relief alongside higher export prices
evidence.facts: ABS September-quarter export prices rose 1.4% q/q and 6.3% y/y; import prices fell 1.1% q/q and rose 5.5% y/y. Export gains included gas +28.6%, coal +4.8% and cereals +5.7%, opposed by ores -6.4% and non-monetary gold -4.8%. Import declines included petroleum -8.7% and fertilisers -20.2%, opposed by office/ADP machines +7.3% and telecom equipment +4.1%. ABS attributes petroleum relief to improving supply during the quarter; this is not proof that current geopolitical threats are resolved. Lower import costs are a fresh offset to the inflation-path argument while export-price resilience supports external incomes. The export/import price ratio improved on these indexes; no national-accounts terms-of-trade actual or private inflow is asserted. Broker AU trade-price series were absent from the focused local snapshot; web calendar forecasts differ and are not treated as a unique consensus.

evidence.title: RBNZ hold surprise and subsequent hawkish offset
evidence.facts: The complete official October 28 record confirms a 4-3 hold at 2.75%, against widely expected October tightening. The majority cited lower-than-expected inflation, smaller indirect fuel-price effects, subdued wages, weak consumption/investment and time to observe two previous hikes. Core near the upper target band and broader price increases were largely expected, rather than evidence of a fresh upside surprise. All members still see tighter policy likely, conditional on the outlook; the record explicitly allows future holds or easing if global demand deteriorates sharply. RNZ reports Westpac economist Eckhold observed the one-year swap rate down about 20 bp after the decision on October 28. That report is an attributed event-time observation, not a new/current October 29 yield measurement. Later conference remarks about further hikes and imported inflation are substantial opposition to weakness. The October 29 Herald interview is now verified separately; this does not verify every scheduled broadcast. Wholesale-to-retail rate pass-through and cost-to-CPI pass-through are distinct; no mechanical rate conclusion is drawn from either.

evidence.title: US Q3 domestic demand remains strong; monthly core persistence offsets quarterly disinflation
evidence.facts: Q3 advance real GDP grew 3.4% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, versus Q2 2.2% and the attributed web survey 3.2%; the broker-model forecast was 1.4% and is not consensus. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. One combined package, not a count of components.

evidence.title: UK household borrowing slows; stronger business lending offsets the downside
evidence.facts: September net house-purchase mortgage approvals fell to 53,400 from revised August 54,800; remortgage approvals rose to 42,600 from 34,000. Net mortgage borrowing slowed to GBP 3.9 bn from revised GBP 4.2 bn, below the prior six-month GBP 4.9 bn average. Net consumer credit fell to GBP 1.9 bn from revised GBP 2.7 bn, slightly below the prior six-month GBP 2.1 bn average. Mortgage borrowing and consumer credit were below broker forecasts GBP 5.363 bn and GBP 2.368 bn; approvals exceeded the broker forecast 50.828k but were slightly below the separately attributed web survey 54.00k. Do not call approvals an unqualified surprise miss. New mortgage effective rates rose to 4.63% from 4.60%. Offsetting household softness, non-financial business bank borrowing rose to GBP 9.3 bn from GBP 4.7 bn, M4Lex net flow rose to GBP 17.0 bn from GBP 9.9 bn and PNFC bank loans to GBP 10.6 bn from GBP 6.4 bn. PNFC total net finance nevertheless slowed to GBP 3.1 bn from GBP 8.5 bn after redemptions/buybacks. M4ex money net flow slowed to GBP 3.9 bn from GBP 16.9 bn. Levels, net flows and annual growth are distinct; this is one release package, not independent votes. September observations predate the October 28 budget and do not measure its effect.

evidence.title: Noon BoJ Outlook resolves the checkpoint without a December promise
evidence.facts: The full Outlook retains conditional further tightening and identifies upside inflation risks. Its detailed analysis finds progress in anchoring inflation near 2%, while household expectations and wage distributions remain uneven. Real consumption is sluggish despite better aggregate income, and procurement costs may not fall with oil benchmarks. These details reinforce structural normalisation without establishing a new rate decision or immediate haven demand.

evidence.title: BoJ holds 1.25%; target-consistent inflation and conditional tightening remain active
evidence.facts: Official decision: 8-1 hold around 1.25%; Takata preferred 1.50% and faster movement toward neutral. Complete Bank View judges underlying CPI generally consistent with 2%, conditions accommodative, and says the Bank will continue raising rates while considering timing/pace against outlook and risks. FY2026/27/28 GDP medians 0.7/0.7/0.8%, changes +0.1/-0.1/0.0 points versus July. Ex-fresh-food CPI 2.5/2.6/2.0%, changes 0.0/+0.2/0.0; ex-fresh-food/energy 2.4/2.7/2.3%, changes -0.1/+0.1/+0.1. Activity risk balanced, price risk upward. Tight labour and wage-price interaction coexist with roughly flat near-term consumption, declining housing and energy/terms-of-trade pressure. Forecasts exclude proposed food-tax cut; possible FY2027 mechanical CPI effect around -1.3 points if implemented is not delivered disinflation. Unanimous ETF annual sales pace rises JPY 330 bn to JPY 860 bn book value from January 2027, about JPY 2460 bn market-value equivalent, with adjustment/suspension flexibility; J-REIT pace remains about JPY 5 bn. One policy package, not independent votes. Hold, target recognition and higher next-year inflation were broadly anticipated in the Reuters preview; no surprise December commitment or measured repricing claimed. Governor conference remains pending.

evidence.title: Ueda conference: anchoring inflation requires adjustment, pace remains data dependent
evidence.facts: Reuters full conference excerpts: underlying inflation consistent 2%, accommodative financial conditions and upside risks justify appropriate adjustment towards neutral. Ueda says sustainability is not yet fully achieved, but the bank will not simply wait; no fixed number of months between hikes. Energy/raw-material pressure is broadening into September/October consumer data; medium/long expectations and next wage bargaining matter. December remains possible, not promised; no published neutral/terminal-rate commitment. Resolves 06:30 UTC material guidance stage after statement/Bank View, rather than renewing a provisional statement-only call.

evidence.title: BoC expected hike and cautious further-tightening path
evidence.facts: The BoC raised 25 bp to 2.50% on October 28, as broadly anticipated. It revised the growth outlook upward, with 2027/2028 GDP around 2%, and projected more persistent inflation: annual-average 2027 inflation about 3%, one percentage point above July, returning to target around mid-2028. Core remains near 2%, CPI excluding gasoline 2.2%, unemployment around 6.5%, excess supply persists and tariffs weigh on Q4. Further increases are conditional and officials will proceed carefully. RBC's October 28 analysis retains a 100 bp total cycle (three further hikes after October) conditional on resilience, while acknowledging no current-data urgency, already-priced term yields and growth downside relative to BoC projections. Financial Post reports Bloomberg-attributed December hike odds falling to 55% after the decision from 100% Tuesday; Canadian Press separately attributes 43% to LSEG Wednesday afternoon. These provider/time snapshots are not interchangeable or a directly refreshed curve. CIBC/Desjardins favour another hike in January and 2.75% peak, illustrating forecast disagreement. Stronger growth/income and a possible longer cycle are support; the reported negative near-term path repricing is material opposition to a current strengthening claim.
evidence.timing_note: Original source date retained. Publication/update hour not independently established; verification does not redate the release.

evidence.title: Canada August payroll falls while weekly earnings growth accelerates
evidence.facts: August payroll employment decreased 49,600 (-0.3%) after July -15,700 (-0.1%); employment rose 0.3% y/y. Losses spanned 10 of 20 sectors. Public administration -22,300 includes federal temporary Census staffing unwinding, so the full headline is not a private-demand collapse. Accommodation/food -6,800, information/culture -5,000, construction -4,500 and retail -4,400 add broader softness. Average weekly earnings rose 0.5% m/m to $1,355 and 3.7% y/y after 3.2%. Earnings mix includes composition, hours, wage and base effects; it is not a pure wage-rate measure. Weekly hours 33.4 were little changed m/m, +0.6% y/y. Vacancies 507,200 and vacancy rate 2.8% were little changed; unemployed per vacancy 2.9 unchanged. One lagged release package, not independent bullish/bearish votes. No unverified consensus surprise is asserted.
evidence.timing_note: Official PDF release clock 8:30 AM Eastern; actual first verified here at 13:40:47 UTC, not observed live at publication.

evidence.title: Lane actual speech recognises European AI growth; annex retains financing and inflation constraints
evidence.facts: Lane says AI already contributes significantly to euro-area growth through adoption and global supply chains, while economywide productivity timing remains uncertain. Corporate contacts report AI adds about 10% to planned capex this year; this is survey evidence, not realised aggregate investment. Tech-goods inflation has limited headline weight. AI firms are more sensitive to monetary tightening through financing needs and capital-market segmentation. European purchases of US technology assets in Q2 are dated portfolio data, not current October 30 flow. Annex retains financing, credit, energy, wage and inflation context with original cutoffs; AI scenarios and a neutral-rate range are not forecasts or a new rate commitment. Speech explicitly does not review yesterday ECB meeting and expresses personal views. Resolves 16:10 UTC Lane stage; growth support is material opposition to mild EUR weakness, but supplies no fresh collective acceleration or evidence that credit/import-energy opposition has disappeared.

SMA collected Oct 12-14, 69 respondents, median DFR 2.50 Oct, 2.75 Dec flat through 2027Q4, 2.50 early 2028, 2.25 late 2028. Stronger Q3 selling prices with some Q4 moderation; ~90% consumer-facing firms report only partial/limited pass-through. Expected wages 3.0 in 26/2.9 in 27, 40% see higher wage demand risk vs 20 but majority no notable effect. No claim Europe has no AI investment; sources explicitly show it. One coherent survey-stage review, not independent vote count.

direction.reason: Retained slight weakening after testing the strongest positive case: today's recovering risk sentiment, the private China PMI beat and the RBA's domestic capacity/inflation concerns support AUD. However, weak Australian factory demand, the official China contraction and fragile technology-related risk appetite still narrowly outweigh those supports for the immediate session. The final PMI revision is small and is not treated as a new major shock. A November hike is widely expected; the evidence does not establish a newly stronger sequence beyond it. Against USD, AUD's greater Chinese-demand and cyclical exposure leaves a slight AUDUSD SELL bias despite USD's own opposition. A sustained broader demand/risk recovery or a materially firmer RBA path defeats this balance. This is a directional backdrop; the user's support touch is not an established entry or a measured break probability.

evidence.title: US Q3 domestic demand remains strong; monthly core persistence offsets quarterly disinflation
evidence.facts: Q3 advance real GDP grew 3.4% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, versus Q2 2.2% and the attributed web survey 3.2%; the broker-model forecast was 1.4% and is not consensus. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. One combined package, not a count of components.

evidence.title: US Q3 domestic demand remains strong; monthly core persistence offsets quarterly disinflation
evidence.facts: Q3 advance real GDP grew 3.4% at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, versus Q2 2.2% and the attributed web survey 3.2%; the broker-model forecast was 1.4% and is not consensus. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, versus 4.6%, supporting genuine private demand apart from inventories, trade and government. Investment included inventory accumulation and information-processing equipment. Exports fell and imports rose; neither is described as an independent bullish vote. Gross domestic purchases prices rose 3.0% annualised, a different measure from the GDP deflator. Quarterly PCE inflation slowed to 2.1% from 5.0%, core to 2.5% from 3.3%. Separately, September monthly headline PCE rose 0.5%, 3.6% y/y; core rose 0.3%, 3.1% y/y. Monthly core matched the 0.3% web survey but exceeded the 0.2% broker forecast. August monthly core was revised from 0.2% to 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.2%, nominal spending 0.5%, real spending less than 0.1% (rounded 0.0%), real disposable income fell 0.3%, and saving rate was 3.8%. August income is now 0.3% and real spending 0.5%; original vintages remain preserved. Strong quarterly private demand and revised monthly core persistence oppose the slower quarterly inflation and softer September household real-income/spending figures. One combined package, not a count of components.

evidence.title: UK household borrowing slows; stronger business lending offsets the downside
evidence.facts: September net house-purchase mortgage approvals fell to 53,400 from revised August 54,800; remortgage approvals rose to 42,600 from 34,000. Net mortgage borrowing slowed to GBP 3.9 bn from revised GBP 4.2 bn, below the prior six-month GBP 4.9 bn average. Net consumer credit fell to GBP 1.9 bn from revised GBP 2.7 bn, slightly below the prior six-month GBP 2.1 bn average. Mortgage borrowing and consumer credit were below broker forecasts GBP 5.363 bn and GBP 2.368 bn; approvals exceeded the broker forecast 50.828k but were slightly below the separately attributed web survey 54.00k. Do not call approvals an unqualified surprise miss. New mortgage effective rates rose to 4.63% from 4.60%. Offsetting household softness, non-financial business bank borrowing rose to GBP 9.3 bn from GBP 4.7 bn, M4Lex net flow rose to GBP 17.0 bn from GBP 9.9 bn and PNFC bank loans to GBP 10.6 bn from GBP 6.4 bn. PNFC total net finance nevertheless slowed to GBP 3.1 bn from GBP 8.5 bn after redemptions/buybacks. M4ex money net flow slowed to GBP 3.9 bn from GBP 16.9 bn. Levels, net flows and annual growth are distinct; this is one release package, not independent votes. September observations predate the October 28 budget and do not measure its effect.

These provider/time snapshots are not interchangeable or a directly refreshed curve. CIBC/Desjardins favour another hike in January and 2.75% peak, illustrating forecast disagreement. Stronger growth/income and a possible longer cycle are support; the reported negative near-term path repricing is material opposition to a current strengthening claim.

evidence.title: RBNZ hold surprise and subsequent hawkish offset
evidence.facts: The complete official October 28 record confirms a 4-3 hold at 2.75%, against widely expected October tightening. The majority cited lower-than -expected inflation, smaller indirect fuel-price effects, subdued wages, weak consumption/investment and time to observe two previous hikes. Core near the upper target band and broader price increases were largely expected, rather than evidence of a fresh upside surprise. All members still see tighter policy likely, conditional on the outlook; the record explicitly allows future holds or easing if global demand deteriorates sharply. RNZ reports Westpac economist Eckhold observed the one-year swap rate down about 20 bp after the decision on October 28. That report is an attributed event-time observation, not a new/current October 29 yield measurement. Later conference remarks about further hikes and imported inflation are substantial opposition to weakness. The October 29 Herald interview is now verified separately; this does not verify every scheduled broadcast. Wholesale-to-retail rate pass-through and cost-to-CPI pass-through are distinct; no mechanical rate conclusion is drawn from either.

evidence.title: Final August wages retain positive real pay; September package is due November 6
evidence.facts: The October 23 MHLW final August release reports total cash earnings +3.9% y/y, scheduled cash earnings +3.8%, and real total pay +1.6% using CPI excluding imputed rent. A separate all-items-CPI deflator gives +2.0%; these are different measures. Common-establishment total pay rose 2.8%, with scheduled pay 3.1%, illustrating composition/sample differences. The earlier October 7 preliminary real-pay +1.5% remains its original vintage. September preliminary wages, including the summer bonus release, are scheduled November 6 at the usual 08:30 JST. September actuals remain unknown.
